content: The Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) was established by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 1991 to regulate the levels of lead and copper in public drinking water at the consumer's tap. This regulation also aimed to minimize the corrosion of pipes caused by water. The rule was developed in response to research demonstrating the harmful effects of lead and copper on human health. To achieve its goals, the LCR required improvements in water treatment processes, assessment of lead and copper levels in households with lead plumbing components, and efforts to eliminate the water source as a contributor to lead and copper contamination. A study conducted by the EPA in 2004-2005 found that the LCR had been effective in 96% of water systems serving populations of at least 3,300 people. In 1993, an article published in the Journal of Environmental Health highlighted that approximately four million lead service line pipes were in use at the time. Lead was historically favored as a material for piping due to its low corrosion rate, which was attributed to the formation of a protective lead carbonate layer on the pipe's surface. However, water with low pH and low calcium levels inhibited the formation of calcium carbonate, and the acidic nature of such water could dissolve lead from the pipes into the water supply. In response to these risks, the Safe Drinking Water Act was amended in 1986 to prohibit the use of lead solders containing more than 0.2% lead and lead pipes containing more than 8% lead. Smaller water suppliers were only required to replace their pipelines if lead or copper levels exceeded the action levels at consumer taps. The action level for lead was set at 0.015 mg/L, while the action level for copper was set at 1.3 mg/L. To comply with the LCR, water suppliers were required to closely monitor water quality and improve it as necessary. Water treatment processes could be adjusted to make the water less corrosive. If a water supplier failed to meet the LCR standards, stricter filtration and monitoring methods were required, and in some cases, lead piping had to be replaced. These revisions became effective on April 11, 2000. Despite its successes, the LCR faced criticism. In 2003, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) investigated the EPA after elevated levels of lead and copper were detected in tap water in the District of Columbia. The GAO found that the EPA had not been collecting sufficient data on lead and copper levels from state water systems, despite claims that these levels had decreased. In fact, data was missing for 72% of water systems. The lack of comprehensive data may have been due to the EPA allocating more resources to lead regulation efforts than to lead reporting.
